lesson.title: Line Symmetry: The Magic Fold Line

steps.say: Have you ever folded a piece of paper in half, cut a shape, and opened it up to find both sides look exactly the same? Let's start with a square piece of paper from art class, eight centimetres on every side. When we fold it, something special happens — the two halves land right on top of each other, perfectly. That perfect matching is what today's whole lesson is about.

visual.caption: A square of art paper, eight centimetres by eight centimetres

steps.say: Here is the big idea. A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves match exactly, like looking in a mirror. Fold our eight centimetre square straight down the middle, and eight divided by two gives four. So we get four centimetres on the left and four centimetres on the right. Same, same. That fold line is a line of symmetry.

visual.caption: Fold down the middle: four centimetres on each side

steps.say: A mirror line also tells us where things land. Imagine a straight strip eight centimetres long, and we fold it right at the four centimetre mark. If you put a little sticker at three centimetres, how far is it from the fold? Four take away three is one centimetre. So its mirror partner sits one centimetre on the other side, at four plus one, which is five centimetres. Equal distance on both sides — that is the mirror rule.

visual.caption: Fold at four: the sticker at three jumps to five, one centimetre each side

steps.say: Now a real example. Your placemat at the kitchen table is a rectangle, twelve centimetres by six centimetres. Fold it side to side: twelve divided by two is six, so you get two pieces that are six by six. That works! Fold it top to bottom: six divided by two is three, so two pieces that are twelve by three. That works too! But a corner to corner fold does not match up on a rectangle. So this placemat has exactly two lines of symmetry.

visual.caption: Rectangle twelve by six: two fold lines that work

steps.say: Let's make it a little harder with a square cedar tile, six centimetres by six centimetres. Fold side to side, six divided by two is three, that works. Fold top to bottom, also three and three, that works. And because all four sides are equal, both corner to corner folds match too! So two straight folds plus two corner folds gives us two plus two, which is four lines of symmetry. A square beats a rectangle.

visual.caption: Square six by six: two middle folds plus two corner folds

steps.say: Here in British Columbia you can see this everywhere in First Peoples art — Coast Salish spindle whorls, woven basket borders, birchbark biting, and even the two sides of a canoe. Artists place a shape on one side of a centre line, then mirror it on the other. Try it with pattern blocks: if you lay three blocks on the left of your fold line, you need three matching blocks on the right. Two groups of three is six blocks in your whole design.

visual.caption: Three blocks on each side of the mirror line: six blocks in all

steps.say: So remember what we counted today. A rectangle placemat had two lines of symmetry, and a square tile had four. Whenever you meet a shape, just ask yourself, can I fold this so both halves land exactly on top of each other? Every fold that works is one more line of symmetry.

visual.caption: Lines of symmetry: rectangle two, square four

lesson.answer: A line of symmetry is a fold line where both halves match exactly — a rectangle has two, a square has four.

practice.question: Ms. Yuanyuan's garden box lid is a rectangle, ninety centimetres long and forty centimetres wide. How many lines of symmetry does it have, and how long is each half when you fold it the long way?
practice.answer: Two lines of symmetry. Folding the long way, ninety divided by two is forty-five, so each half is forty-five centimetres by forty centimetres.
